name: Coding–decoding
analogy: Treat a coded word like a message with a repeatable rule. Compare each letter’s position before guessing.
explain: Check forward or backward shifts, alternating shifts, reversal, and alphabet positions. Verify the same rule against every example before applying it.
formulas: Check whether the whole word is reversed

variant.q: If CAT is coded as DBU by shifting each letter forward once, how is DOG coded?
variant.solution: D→E, O→P, and G→H, so DOG becomes EPH.

name: Number and letter series
analogy: A series has a rhythm. Write the changes between terms to make its rhythm visible.
explain: Test constant differences, ratios, squares or cubes, alternating subsequences, and second differences. For letters, convert positions to numbers first.

variant.solution: Each term doubles, so the next term is 24 × 2 = 48.

name: Analogy
analogy: Name the relationship in the first pair, then apply exactly that relationship to the second pair.
explain: Common links include tool and use, part and whole, worker and workplace, cause and effect, and opposites. State the link in words before selecting an option.
formulas: Check the direction of the relationship
Eliminate options with only a loose association

variant.solution: A pen is used to write; a knife is used to cut.

name: Classification and odd one out
analogy: Find the shared property of most items; the outlier is the one that breaks that rule.
explain: Check category, divisibility, prime or square status, letter positions, and word structure. Use the simplest rule that explains all but one item.
formulas: Confirm the rule covers every item

variant.solution: 9 is composite; the remaining numbers are prime.

name: Blood relations
analogy: Turn the sentence into a small family tree instead of holding every relationship in your head.
explain: Start from the speaker, mark each generation and gender, and translate possessive phrases one link at a time. Resolve pronouns only after drawing the chain.
formulas: Parent → child moves down one generation
Maternal and paternal name the parent’s side
Mark gender when it is stated

variant.q: Pointing to a woman, a man says, ‘She is my mother’s only daughter.’ How is she related to him?
variant.solution: His mother’s daughter is his sister (unless the speaker is the daughter, which the prompt identifies as a man).

name: Direction sense
analogy: Track each move on a compass grid. Turns change facing; moves change position.
explain: Record north/south and east/west displacement separately. Use the Pythagorean theorem for straight-line distance and re-check left/right relative to the person’s current facing.

variant.q: Walk 3 km east, then 4 km north. How far are you from the start in a straight line?
variant.solution: The moves are perpendicular, so distance = √(3² + 4²) = 5 km.

name: Ranking and order
analogy: A queue gives two views of the same line: count from the front and from the back without counting the person twice.
explain: Use total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1. For swaps, translate the changed position back to the person’s original position carefully.

variant.q: Anu is 12th from the top and 18th from the bottom. How many students are there?

name: Seating arrangements
analogy: Treat each clue as a constraint. Place fixed positions first, then fit the remaining people.
explain: Draw numbered seats, record whether people face inward or outward, and distinguish immediate neighbours from people merely somewhere to one side. Check every clue after arranging.
formulas: Place fixed ends and middle positions first
For circles, fix one person to remove rotation duplicates
Facing outward reverses left and right

variant.q: A, B, C, D, E sit in a row. C is in the middle, A at the left end, E at the right end, and B is left of C. Who sits between C and E?
variant.solution: The order must be A, B, C, D, E, so D is between C and E.

name: Calendar
analogy: Weekdays repeat in a seven-day cycle, so only the remainder after dividing by seven changes the day.
explain: Count odd days modulo 7. For dates, account for leap years and the exact interval endpoints before adding the remainder.
formulas: Days later: add n mod 7 weekdays

variant.q: If today is Wednesday, what day will it be after 100 days?
variant.solution: 100 mod 7 = 2; two days after Wednesday is Friday.

name: Clock problems
analogy: Clock hands move at different speeds. Convert the question to angles or minutes before solving.
explain: The minute hand moves 6° per minute and the hour hand 0.5° per minute. For gain/loss clocks, calculate the steady error rate over the stated real duration.

variant.q: A clock loses 5 minutes every hour. How much time does it lose in 12 real hours?
variant.solution: At 5 minutes lost per hour, 12 hours gives 5 × 12 = 60 minutes.

name: Dice and cubes
analogy: Compare two views of a die by keeping one face fixed and tracking which faces meet it.
explain: Faces seen together are adjacent, never opposite. With two views sharing a face, compare the rotation; for painted cubes, count faces by edge and corner position.
formulas: A face’s opposite never touches it
For a standard die, opposite faces sum to 7

variant.q: On a standard die, 1 is opposite 6 and 2 is opposite 5. Which face is opposite 3?
variant.solution: The remaining pair is 3 and 4, so 4 is opposite 3.

name: Mathematical operations
analogy: If symbols have been reassigned, translate them to their defined operations before using normal order of operations.
explain: Substitute every symbol first, then apply BODMAS. For number-interchange puzzles, swap the values before evaluating.
formulas: Rewrite the expression using the given meanings
Then apply brackets and operation precedence
Check whether the symbols or values were redefined

name: Syllogisms and deduction
analogy: Use overlapping circles to test whether a conclusion must be true for every arrangement allowed by the statements.
explain: Treat statements as the full set of facts. A conclusion follows only when it is guaranteed; possibility alone is not enough. ‘Some’ does not imply ‘all’.
formulas: All A are B means A is inside B
Some A are B means overlap exists

variant.q: All roses are flowers. All flowers fade. Does ‘All roses fade’ follow?
variant.solution: Roses are within flowers, and flowers are within things that fade. Therefore all roses fade.

name: Non-verbal reasoning
analogy: Compare shapes by tracking one feature at a time: rotation, reflection, count, shading, or position.
explain: For a sequence, note the change between consecutive figures. A mirror reverses left and right; a rotation turns the whole figure while keeping relative positions.
formulas: Mirror reflection swaps left and right

variant.q: In a vertical mirror, the lowercase letter b is reflected as which letter?
variant.solution: A vertical mirror reverses left and right, so b appears as d.

name: Logical sequence of words
analogy: Put events in the order they happen in the real world, such as seed, plant, flower, fruit.
explain: Look for chronological order, cause and effect, increasing size, or steps in a process. State the ordering rule before choosing the option.

variant.q: Arrange the stages: 1. Seed  2. Plant  3. Flower  4. Fruit
variant.solution: The natural order is seed, plant, flower, then fruit.

name: Logical Venn diagrams
analogy: Use nested circles for ‘inside’ relationships and overlapping circles for groups that share some members.
explain: Translate the words into set relationships. If two groups are distinct kinds within a larger group, draw both inside the larger circle without overlapping them.
formulas: A subset of B: A inside B

variant.q: Which relationship fits Dogs, Animals, and Cats?
options: Separate Dogs and Cats circles inside Animals
variant.solution: Dogs and cats are distinct groups; both belong inside the larger Animals group.
